prompt.context: Our client is a third-party company that manages online bill pay on behalf of banks. They are not a bank themselves. The client earns $0.50 per Online Bill Pay transaction and $1.00 per Online Check transaction (where a physical check is sent). The bank pays these transaction fees. The core benefit to the bank is customer retention — customers who use online bill pay are more likely to stay with the bank for many years. Currently, 70% of the population has online banking, but only a small portion of this group actually pays a bill through their online bank account.
prompt.question: The client has come to McKinsey to help figure out how they can increase the number of people using the online bill pay feature. How would you approach this problem?

clarifying_info.a: The bank pays the transaction fee to our client.

clarifying_info.q: What does the client earn per transaction?
clarifying_info.a: $0.50 per Online Bill Pay and $1.00 per Online Check.
No, the client is a third party who manages the online bill pay process for the bank.

clarifying_info.q: What is the core benefit to the bank?
clarifying_info.a: Customer retention — those who use online bill pay are more likely to stay with the bank long-term.

framework: Market and Customers: understand the larger market and trends — what drives consumer behavior, the competitive landscape (other banks and substitutes such as other online or non-online bill paying services)
Customers WITH Online Bank Accounts: identify barriers preventing these customers from using the online bill pay feature and ways to increase their usage
Customers WITHOUT Online Bank Accounts: identify barriers preventing these customers from getting signed up online and strategies to bring them into online banking

questions.prompt: What barriers might prevent customers WITHOUT online bank accounts from using online bill pay?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate lists at least 4 of these barriers: (1) Perception that online banking is too difficult or complex to use (e.g., elderly population); (2) Lack of internet access; (3) Loyalty to other online payment programs or auto-debit; (4) Lack of a bank account altogether; (5) Language challenges — population accustomed to the internet but on customized websites, relevant for the growing Hispanic population; (6) Fear of security issues.

questions.prompt: Why might someone WITH an online bank account NOT use the bill pay function?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate lists at least 4 of these reasons: (1) Lack of awareness of the feature; (2) Habit or loyalty to other online bill pay programs; (3) Do not pay any bills online — fear of security; (4) Time required to input company names and payment information into the banking account system before bills can be paid; (5) Banks with multiple institutions who prefer the flexibility of choosing which bank to pay from (e.g., switching checking accounts monthly, or storing all accounts at amex.com); (6) Language issues.

questions.prompt: You are given growth data for online bill pay over the past 5 years. What do you notice? (5 years ago: 50% had online banking, 10% paid online bills occasionally, 5% were active online bill payers. Today: 70% have online banking, 20% pay online bills occasionally, 7% are active online bill payers.) What does this tell us?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize three things: (1) Total people with online banking is growing; (2) Those using online bill pay occasionally has doubled (10% to 20%); (3) Those becoming active bill payers are growing at a slower rate (5% to 7% — only 40% growth vs. 100% growth for occasional users). The key extrapolation: while more people are starting to pay bills occasionally, fewer are converting into active users. This is bad news for the client because active users drive recurring transaction revenue.

math.setup: Compare growth rates: occasional users 10%→20% (100% increase); active users 5%→7% (40% increase). The conversion rate from occasional to active is declining.
steps: Conversion gap is widening — occasional users are not becoming active users at the same pace
math.answer: The conversion rate from occasional to active bill payer is declining, which is bad for client revenue.

questions.prompt: Why might the conversion rate from occasional to active bill payer be declining?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate lists at least 2 of these reasons: (1) Decline in customer service or user experience; (2) Increased loyalty to competing online payment systems; (3) Five years ago, those engaging in any online bill pay were 'early adopters' who were tech-savvy and more likely to convert at a higher rate — this population has been exhausted and the newer wave of occasional users is less inclined to convert.

questions.prompt: It is clear the value proposition needs to be improved. How would you improve it to increase conversion from occasional to active bill payers?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate lists at least 3 of the following value proposition improvements: (1) Sending out reminders for bills due; (2) Offering financing for bill payment; (3) Bundling all bills together with a 'one-click' payment system; (4) Offering incentives to use online bill pay; (5) Offering recommendations on better products once the system can see what the customer pays each month.

brainstorming.prompt: What improvements to the value proposition could convert occasional online bill payers into active bill payers?

categories.name: Convenience / UX
ideas: Pre-populate payee information to reduce setup time

categories.name: Financial Incentives
ideas: Rewards or cashback for using online bill pay
Discounts or waived fees for active users

categories.name: Personalization / Insights
ideas: Recommendations on better products or services based on spending patterns
Spending summaries and financial health dashboards

categories.name: Accessibility / Awareness
ideas: Awareness campaigns targeted at online bankers not using bill pay
Simplified onboarding for less tech-savvy users

recommendation: First, focus on customers who already have online banking but are not using bill pay regularly — improve the value proposition and user experience so that occasional bill payers convert to active bill payers. This must be done first; without improving this conversion step, newly onboarded users will also fail to become active.
Second, once the occasional-to-active conversion is fixed, work on converting all online banking customers into at least occasional online bill payers.
Third, expand the online banking base itself — aim to bring 100% of bank account holders onto online banking, which expands the top of the funnel.
risks: If the conversion problem (occasional → active) is not fixed first, acquiring more occasional users will not improve revenue.
Competitive online payment platforms (e.g., direct-pay portals, third-party apps) may continue to attract users away.
Security concerns and lack of awareness remain structural barriers for certain customer segments.
next_steps: Conduct customer research to identify the top reasons occasional users do not become active — prioritize UX fixes and feature development accordingly.
Pilot value proposition improvements (e.g., one-click payment, bill reminders, incentives) and measure conversion lift.
Work with bank partners to launch awareness campaigns targeting online banking customers not yet using bill pay.
